name: PRP facial (vampire facial)

lead: A PRP facial, popularly the vampire facial, uses plasma concentrated from your own blood, applied during microneedling, to rejuvenate skin: smoother texture, softer fine lines and improved acne scars.

PRP is blood plasma with red cells removed and platelets raised to about three to five times normal levels. Proponents say its growth factors signal skin cells to repair tissue and build collagen, while microneedling creates controlled micro-injuries that start healing. Reviews describe PRP evidence as mixed across conditions, and small studies exist for skin rejuvenation.

paras: A clinician draws a small blood sample, spins it in a centrifuge and applies the plasma to the face, most often with microneedling. Some do-it-yourself communities also describe home versions. Redness and swelling settle within days, and people usually repeat sessions.

Redness, swelling, bruising and numbness are usually brief. The main documented harm is infection from unlicensed providers using inadequately sterilised equipment: in 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to an Albuquerque spa, after a 2018 state warning. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, though the preparation devices need clearance.

chain: Better texture, fewer fine lines and scars
angle.text: Users have PRP facials, popularly the vampire facial, for rejuvenated skin, smoother texture, fewer fine lines and softer acne scars. Your own platelets applied with microneedling are said to trigger skin repair and a collagen response. Small studies exist for skin rejuvenation.

lead: A PRP facial, popularly known as a vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure in which blood drawn from the patient is centrifuged to produce platelet-rich plasma (PRP), which is then applied to the face, most often together with microneedling. It is marketed for skin rejuvenation, fine lines, texture and acne scars.[1][2]

PRP is a concentrate of plasma from a person's own blood with red blood cells removed and platelets kept, usually raised to about three to five times normal levels. Its evidence base is described as mixed: it appears to help in some conditions and not in others, and facial rejuvenation is one of several aesthetic uses with limited support.[1] Side effects such as redness, swelling and bruising are typically brief.[2]

The main documented harm is infection transmission when procedures are performed by unlicensed operators. New Mexico health officials warned in 2018 about a business offering vampire facials, and in 2024 the CDC reported that three women had been diagnosed with HIV after treatments at an Albuquerque spa.[1][2] The treatment has also been discussed in looksmaxxing forums, including by members who describe doing PRP microneedling themselves.[3]
infobox: Skin texture, fine lines, scars, glow
PRP not regulated by FDA; preparation devices require clearance[1]

paras: Blood is drawn, spun in a centrifuge and separated so that a plasma fraction rich in platelets remains. It may be activated before use, though activation is not required.[1] The product is applied to the skin during or after microneedling, or injected. The practice sits within the older category of autologous blood therapy, which dermatologists used widely in the early twentieth century before abandoning it for lack of evidence; interest returned in the 2000s.[2]

The term platelet-rich plasma was first used in 1954, platelet banks followed in the 1960s, and it entered surgical use in the late 1980s and hair-loss research in 2006.[1] Vampire facials became popular in the 2010s after celebrity endorsements.[1] A 2024 study used Google Trends data to examine how social media affected the popularity of the vampire facial.[4]

PRP contains growth factors and cytokines. Proponents say microneedling and PRP together stimulate collagen production, and clinicians have published technique descriptions such as a single-handed method for combining the two.[5]

Reported effects include redness, swelling, bruising and numbness, usually resolving within about two days, though some people have taken a week or more.[2] The central safety concern is providers without infection-control training. In 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that at least one business offering vampire facials could potentially spread HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and in 2024 the CDC announced that three women treated at an Albuquerque spa had been diagnosed with HIV. Officials found the operator was unlicensed and had reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment without sterilisation; about 200 other former clients tested negative.[1][2]

Published literature specific to the vampire facial found in the sources reviewed consists of a 2021 technique paper on combining microneedling with PRP[5] and a 2024 analysis of its online popularity,[4] neither of which reports efficacy outcomes. Wikipedia's overview of PRP describes evidence across conditions as mixed and reports positive studies for hair loss and for some wounds, while stating that claims for some aesthetic uses lack supporting evidence.[1] The sources reviewed do not report large randomised trials establishing the size or durability of facial benefit.

In the United States the FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so its clinical use is considered off-label, while the devices used to prepare it require FDA clearance.[1] Intramuscular PRP injections were removed from the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list in 2011.[1]

A looksmax.org member has posted about ordering equipment for a home setup to perform PRP vampire facials and related PRF 'biofiller' preparations.[3] Replies in the thread are largely jokes. Clinicians and health agencies, in contrast, emphasise licensed settings because of infection risk.[1][2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the vampire facial appears mainly in posts by members planning to prepare PRP and PRF 'biofillers' for personal use.[3]

claims.claim: PRP microneedling can improve skin quality and slow visible ageing.
Doing PRP at home or in a self-run setup is a workable alternative to a clinic.
